---
title: "Survival weights and the time grid: a caution for ipw 1.3.2 and earlier"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(ipw)
library(survival)
stored <- readRDS("survival-weights-time-grid.rds")
cases <- stored$cases
data("haartdat", package = "ipw")
cases$haartdat_first$data <- haartdat
cases$haartdat_cens$data <- haartdat
versions <- names(stored$by_version)
old_res <- function(v, nm) stored$by_version[[v]]$results[[nm]]
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) trimws(formatC(x, format = "g", digits = d))
```

## Summary

In ipw 1.3.2 and earlier, `ipwtm()` with `family = "survival"` and
`type = "first"` (or `"cens"` for censoring weights) gives correct weights
**only when the data are on a full time grid**: all follow-up is split at
all times that occur in the data, so that the rows of all subjects start and
end at the same time points. This is how the data are prepared in the
examples of the JSS paper (van der Wal and Geskus, 2011), in `haartdat` and
in Example 2 of `?ipwtm`.

* **Caution for older versions.** If the rows of different subjects end at
  different times, for example one row per visit with each subject's own
  visit dates, ipw 1.3.2 and earlier give incorrect weights. The probability
  of each row uses the increase in the baseline hazard since the previous
  time point *in the whole data set*, which is the start of the row only on
  a full grid. All `r length(versions)` versions on CRAN, from ipw 1.0 (2011)
  to 1.3.2, behave the same way.
* **If you used an older version with data on the full grid, your weights
  are correct.** To be sure, check your data with `rows_affected()`
  (section 5), or rerun the analysis with the updated ipw, which gives the
  same weights for such data (section 8).
* **Improvement in this version.** Each row now uses the baseline hazard
  over its own interval `(tstart, timevar]`, so data with individual visit
  times can be used directly, without splitting them onto a grid.
* With individual visit times the older versions' weights can be far off: in
  the example in section 6 some differ from the correct ones by a factor of
  more than 30, and in a simulation with a known answer (section 7) ipw
  1.2.1.1 gave the same biased estimate as using no weights at all, while the
  updated version gives the right answer.

## 1. Hazards in plain words

**Hazard.** The hazard is the risk that the event happens *right now*, for
someone to whom it has not happened yet. Here the event is the start of
treatment (or drop-out, for censoring weights). It is a rate, like a speed:
a hazard of 0.01 per day means roughly a 1% chance of starting on the next
day, for someone who has not started yet.

**Cumulative hazard.** The cumulative hazard $H(t)$ is the hazard added up
over time, as distance is speed added up over time. The risk built up over a
stretch of time, for example from day 10 to day 20, is $H(20) - H(10)$, and

$$
P(\text{no event from day 10 to day 20}) = \exp\{-[H(20) - H(10)]\},
$$

so the probability of the event is one minus this. A small amount of hazard
gives a probability close to 0, a large amount a probability close to 1.

**Cox model.** A Cox model splits the hazard of a person into two parts:

$$
\text{hazard of a person} = \underbrace{h_0(t)}_{\text{baseline: the same for everyone, changes over time}} \times \underbrace{r = e^{\beta^\top x}}_{\text{relative risk: personal, from the covariates}}
$$

**How the baseline hazard is estimated.** The cumulative baseline hazard
$H_0(t)$ only goes up at the times when someone has the event. At such a
time it goes up by

$$
\frac{\text{number of events at that time}}{\text{sum of } r \text{ over everyone still at risk at that time}}
$$

where "at risk" means followed at that time and not yet exposed. (With
several events at the same time, Efron's method, which `coxph()` uses,
adjusts the denominator slightly.) One event among people with a high total
risk is not surprising, so the step is small; one event among people with a
low total risk is surprising, so the step is large.

**From hazard to weight.** For one row of a patient covering
`(tstart, timevar]`: take the baseline hazard over the row,
$H_0(t) - H_0(t_\text{start})$; multiply by the patient's $r$ to get the
patient's hazard over the row; turn it into the probability of what actually
happened (exposure or no exposure); the weight is the inverse of that
probability, multiplied over the rows of the patient so far. Section 4 does
this step by step for three patients.

## 2. What the weights should be

For `type = "first"`, each row of a subject covers an interval
`(tstart, timevar]` until the first exposure (for example the start of a
treatment). With a Cox model for the time to exposure, the probability of
*no* exposure during the row is

$$
P(\text{no exposure in } (t_\text{start}, t]) =
\exp\{-[H_0(t) - H_0(t_\text{start})]\, e^{\beta^\top x}\},
$$

where $H_0$ is the cumulative baseline hazard. The probability of exposure
at the end of the row is one minus this. The weight of a row is the product
of the inverse probabilities of the rows of that subject so far (and the
numerator model's probabilities, for stabilised weights). Censoring weights
(`type = "cens"`) use the probability of remaining uncensored the same way.

## 3. What older versions computed, and why the full grid matters

Older versions computed the hazard of a row as

$$
H_0(t) - H_0(t_\text{prev}),
$$

where $t_\text{prev}$ is the time point just before $t$ **among all times
in the data**, of any subject. When the data are on a full grid (every subject has
rows at the same time points), $t_\text{prev}$ is the start of the row, and
the two are the same: the older versions are correct. When subjects have
their own visit times, $t_\text{prev}$ is usually later than
$t_\text{start}$, so part of the hazard during the row is left out: the
probability of no exposure is too high and the probability of exposure too
low. Weights of exposed rows come out too large, and weights of unexposed
rows too small.

## 4. A worked example with three patients

```{r tiny-data}
d <- cases$tiny$data
d
```

Patients 1 and 3 are at risk from day 10 and day 5 to day 20. Patient 2 is
exposed at day 15 and patient 1 at day 20, so the baseline hazard increases
at day 15 and at day 20. The times in the data are 5, 10, 15 and 20.

The Cox model and its cumulative baseline hazard. Here $H_0$ is computed by
hand from the risk sets (Efron's method, as `coxph()` uses), without
`basehaz()` or `survfit()`:

```{r tiny-fit}
fit <- coxph(Surv(tstart, time, a) ~ l, data = d, ties = "efron")
r <- exp(coef(fit) * d$l)                    # relative hazard of each row

# Efron cumulative baseline hazard from the risk sets
H_efron <- function(start, stop, event, r) {
  et <- sort(unique(stop[event == 1]))
  inc <- vapply(et, function(t) {
    S0 <- sum(r[start < t & stop >= t])      # risk set at time t
    D <- which(stop == t & event == 1)       # events at time t
    k <- length(D)
    sum(1 / (S0 - (seq_len(k) - 1) / k * sum(r[D])))
  }, numeric(1))
  cum <- cumsum(inc)
  function(t) vapply(t, function(s) {
    j <- which(et <= s)
    if (length(j)) cum[max(j)] else 0
  }, numeric(1))
}
H0 <- H_efron(d$tstart, d$time, d$a, r)
H0(c(5, 10, 15, 20))
```

### Step by step

```{r tiny-steps, include = FALSE}
b <- unname(coef(fit))
at_risk_15 <- which(d$tstart < 15 & d$time >= 15)
at_risk_20 <- which(d$tstart < 20 & d$time >= 20 & !(d$time == 15))
step15 <- 1 / sum(r[at_risk_15])
step20 <- 1 / sum(r[at_risk_20])
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
```

**Relative risks.** The Cox model gives $\beta = `r round(b, 2)`$ for `l`
(higher `l`, lower risk; with three patients this is just how the data fell),
so each row has relative risk $r = e^{`r round(b, 2)` \times l}$:

```{r tiny-r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(patient = d$id,
                        row = paste0("(", d$tstart, ", ", d$time, "]"),
                        l = d$l, r = r), digits = 3)
```

**The baseline hazard.** It goes up only on day 15 (patient 2 is exposed)
and day 20 (patient 1 is exposed):

* Day 15: at risk are the rows `r paste0("(", d$tstart[at_risk_15], ", ", d$time[at_risk_15], "]", collapse = ", ")`
  of patients `r paste(d$id[at_risk_15], collapse = ", ")`. Step =
  1 / (`r paste(f3(r[at_risk_15]), collapse = " + ")`) = **`r f3(step15)`**.
* Day 20: patient 2 is no longer at risk; at risk are the rows
  `r paste0("(", d$tstart[at_risk_20], ", ", d$time[at_risk_20], "]", collapse = ", ")`
  of patients `r paste(d$id[at_risk_20], collapse = " and ")`. Step =
  1 / (`r paste(f3(r[at_risk_20]), collapse = " + ")`) = **`r f3(step20)`**.

So $H_0$ is 0 up to day 15, `r f3(step15)` from day 15 and
`r f3(step15 + step20)` from day 20, as computed above.

**One row: patient 1 from day 10 to day 20, exposed at day 20.**

1. Baseline hazard over the row: $H_0(20) - H_0(10)$ =
   `r f3(H0(20))` − `r f3(H0(10))` = `r f3(H0(20) - H0(10))`.
2. Hazard of patient 1 over the row: × $r$ = `r f3(H0(20) - H0(10))` ×
   `r f3(r[2])` = **`r f3((H0(20) - H0(10)) * r[2])`**.
3. Probability of exposure in the row: $1 - e^{-`r f3((H0(20) - H0(10)) * r[2])`}$ =
   `r f3(1 - exp(-(H0(20) - H0(10)) * r[2]))`.
4. Weight: the first row (day 0 to 10) has no hazard, so its probability of
   no exposure is 1; the weight is 1 / `r f3(1 - exp(-(H0(20) - H0(10)) * r[2]))` =
   **`r f3(1 / (1 - exp(-(H0(20) - H0(10)) * r[2])))`**.

**What the old versions did with the same row.** In step 1 they did not use
$H_0(20) - H_0(10)$. The time just before day 20 among all times in the data
is day 15 (the end of patient 2's row), so they used
$H_0(20) - H_0(15)$ = `r f3(H0(20))` − `r f3(H0(15))` = `r f3(H0(20) - H0(15))`:
the step of `r f3(step15)` on day 15 was left out, although patient 1 was
followed on that day. Then the hazard is
`r f3((H0(20) - H0(15)) * r[2])` instead of `r f3((H0(20) - H0(10)) * r[2])`,
the probability of exposure `r f3(1 - exp(-(H0(20) - H0(15)) * r[2]))` instead of
`r f3(1 - exp(-(H0(20) - H0(10)) * r[2]))`, and the weight
`r f3(1 / (1 - exp(-(H0(20) - H0(15)) * r[2])))` instead of
`r f3(1 / (1 - exp(-(H0(20) - H0(10)) * r[2])))`. A hazard that is too small
makes the probability of an exposure too small, so the weight of an exposed
row too large; for an unexposed row it makes the probability of *no*
exposure too large, so the weight too small.

### All rows

For each row, the correct hazard uses `tstart`; the old one used the
previous time in the data:

```{r tiny-table}
times <- sort(unique(d$time))
t_prev <- c(NA, times)[match(d$time, times)]
hz_correct <- (H0(d$time) - H0(d$tstart)) * r
hz_old <- (H0(d$time) - ifelse(is.na(t_prev), 0, H0(t_prev))) * r
p_correct <- ifelse(d$a == 1, 1 - exp(-hz_correct), exp(-hz_correct))
p_old <- ifelse(d$a == 1, 1 - exp(-hz_old), exp(-hz_old))
w_correct <- ave(1 / p_correct, d$id, FUN = cumprod)
w_old <- ave(1 / p_old, d$id, FUN = cumprod)

tab <- data.frame(id = d$id, interval = paste0("(", d$tstart, ", ", d$time, "]"),
                  old_interval = paste0("(", ifelse(is.na(t_prev), "-", t_prev), ", ", d$time, "]"),
                  hazard_correct = hz_correct, hazard_old = hz_old,
                  weight_correct = w_correct, weight_old = w_old)
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 3)
```

The rows `(10, 20]` of patient 1 and `(5, 20]` of patient 3 were at risk at
day 15, when patient 2 was exposed, but the old calculation started counting
at day 15 and missed that part of the hazard. Patient 1, exposed at day 20,
gets a weight of `r round(w_old[2], 3)` instead of `r round(w_correct[2], 3)`.

The same numbers from the package. Every old version gives the old weights,
and the development version gives the correct ones:

```{r tiny-package}
w_dev <- ipwtm(exposure = a, family = "survival", denominator = ~ l, id = id,
               tstart = tstart, timevar = time, type = "first", data = d)$ipw.weights
data.frame(id = d$id, interval = tab$interval,
           ipw_1.2.1.1 = old_res("1.2.1.1", "tiny")$weights,
           ipw_1.3.2 = old_res("1.3.2", "tiny")$weights,
           this_version = w_dev, by_hand = w_correct)
```

```{r tiny-checks}
# old versions = the old calculation above; this version = the correct one
max(abs(old_res("1.0", "tiny")$weights - w_old))
max(abs(w_dev - w_correct))
```

## 5. Were my data on the full grid?

For the older versions, what matters is whether each row that enters the
exposure (or censoring) model starts at the time point just before its
`timevar` among all times in the data. This function counts the rows for
which that is *not* the case; 0 means the data are on the full grid and the
older versions gave correct weights:

```{r check-fun}
rows_affected <- function(data, id, tstart, timevar, exposure) {
  d <- data[order(data[[id]], data[[timevar]]), ]
  in_model <- ave(d[[exposure]], d[[id]], FUN = function(z) cumsum(cumsum(z)) <= 1) == 1
  times <- sort(unique(d[[timevar]]))
  t_prev <- c(-Inf, times)[match(d[[timevar]], times)]
  first_time <- d[[timevar]] == times[1]
  sum(in_model & !first_time & d[[tstart]] != t_prev)
}
rows_affected(haartdat, "patient", "tstart", "fuptime", "haartind")
rows_affected(cases$own_first$data, "id", "tstart", "time", "a")
nrow(cases$own_first$data)
```

`haartdat` is on the full grid: all patients have rows every 100 days. In
the data with individual visit times nearly every row is off the grid. Run
`rows_affected()` on the data you gave to `ipwtm()`, with the names of your
id, start time, end time and exposure (or censoring) columns.

### The examples of the JSS paper

The JSS paper's example on tuberculosis and mortality (Section 4.3, Example 2
of `?ipwtm`) has CD4 measurements at irregular times, a different schedule
for each patient (`timedat`). Those measurements are only used to fit a CD4
model. The data given to `ipwtm()` are built on a full grid: every patient
gets a row at every TB time and every end of follow-up of *all* patients.

```{r jss-grid}
data("basdat", package = "ipw")
data("timedat", package = "ipw")
# CD4 measurement times: each patient has their own
head(timedat$fuptime[timedat$id == 2], 6)
head(timedat$fuptime[timedat$id == 3], 6)

# the data for ipwtm(), as in Example 2 of ?ipwtm
times <- sort(unique(c(basdat$Ttb, basdat$Tend)))
startstop <- data.frame(id = rep(basdat$id, each = length(times)),
                        fuptime = rep(times, nrow(basdat)))
startstop <- merge(startstop, basdat, by = "id", all.x = TRUE)
startstop <- startstop[with(startstop, fuptime <= Tend), ]
startstop$tstart <- tstartfun(id, fuptime, startstop)
startstop$tb <- ifelse(with(startstop, !is.na(Ttb) & fuptime >= Ttb), 1, 0)
head(startstop[startstop$id == 2, c("id", "tstart", "fuptime", "tb")], 6)
head(startstop[startstop$id == 3, c("id", "tstart", "fuptime", "tb")], 6)
rows_affected(startstop, "id", "tstart", "fuptime", "tb")
```

Patients 2 and 3 have identical rows, cut at other patients' TB and end
times, and no row is off the grid: the older versions give correct weights
for this example. Had the rows instead been cut at each patient's own CD4
measurement times, almost every row would have been off the grid:

```{r jss-visits}
visits <- merge(timedat[, c("id", "fuptime")], basdat[, c("id", "Ttb")], by = "id")
visits <- visits[order(visits$id, visits$fuptime), ]
visits$tstart <- tstartfun(id, fuptime, visits)
visits$tb <- ifelse(!is.na(visits$Ttb) & visits$fuptime >= visits$Ttb, 1, 0)
rows_affected(visits, "id", "tstart", "fuptime", "tb")
nrow(visits)
```

## 6. All versions from 1.0 to 1.3.2

The same cases were run in every version of ipw on CRAN (in separate R
sessions, with the script `data-raw/make-survival-time-grid-article-data.R`) and
compared with the correct weights computed by hand as above:

* **haartdat**: treatment weights (`type = "first"`) and censoring weights
  (`type = "cens"`) from the `?ipwtm` example; on the full grid.
* **own times**: 300 subjects, each with their own visit times, unstabilised
  (`numerator = NULL`) and stabilised (`numerator = ~ x`), and censoring
  weights.
* **own times on the full grid**: the same data, with every row split at
  all times in the data (as in Example 2 of `?ipwtm`).

```{r correct-weights, include = FALSE}
correct_weights <- function(d, exposure, id, tstart, time, num, den, type) {
  o <- order(d[[id]], d[[time]])
  ds <- d[o, ]
  ev <- ds[[exposure]]
  sel <- ave(ev, ds[[id]], FUN = function(z) cumsum(cumsum(z)) <= 1) == 1
  prob <- function(covs) {
    if (is.null(covs)) return(rep(1, nrow(ds)))
    act <- ds[sel, ]
    f <- as.formula(paste0("Surv(", tstart, ", ", time, ", ", exposure, ") ~ ",
                           paste(covs, collapse = " + ")))
    m <- coxph(f, data = act, ties = "efron")
    X <- model.matrix(as.formula(paste("~", paste(covs, collapse = " + "))), ds)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
    rr <- drop(exp(X %*% coef(m)))
    H <- H_efron(act[[tstart]], act[[time]], ev[sel], rr[sel])
    dH <- (H(ds[[time]]) - H(ds[[tstart]])) * rr
    p <- if (type == "cens") exp(-dH) else ifelse(ev == 1, 1 - exp(-dH), exp(-dH))
    p[!sel] <- 1
    p
  }
  w <- ave(prob(num) / prob(den), ds[[id]], FUN = cumprod)
  w[order(o)]
}
refs <- list(
  haartdat_first = correct_weights(haartdat, "haartind", "patient", "tstart", "fuptime",
                                   c("sex", "age"), c("sex", "age", "cd4.sqrt"), "first"),
  haartdat_cens = correct_weights(haartdat, "dropout", "patient", "tstart", "fuptime",
                                  c("sex", "age"), c("sex", "age", "cd4.sqrt"), "cens"),
  own_first = correct_weights(cases$own_first$data, "a", "id", "tstart", "time",
                              NULL, c("x", "l"), "first"),
  own_first_stab = correct_weights(cases$own_first_stab$data, "a", "id", "tstart", "time",
                                   "x", c("x", "l"), "first"),
  own_cens = correct_weights(cases$own_cens$data, "dropout", "id", "tstart", "time",
                             "x", c("x", "l"), "cens"),
  common_grid_first = correct_weights(cases$common_grid_first$data, "a", "id", "tstart", "time",
                                      NULL, c("x", "l"), "first"))
now <- lapply(cases[names(refs)], function(cs) eval(cs$call, list(data = cs$data))$ipw.weights)
```

```{r versions-table, echo = FALSE}
status <- function(x, ref) {
  if (is.null(x)) return("not run")
  if (!is.na(x$error)) return(if (grepl("No type specified", x$error)) "no type = \"cens\"" else "error")
  d <- max(abs(x$weights / ref - 1))
  if (d < 1e-8) "correct" else paste0("incorrect (", fmt(d), ")")
}
labels <- c(haartdat_first = "haartdat, first", haartdat_cens = "haartdat, cens",
            own_first = "own times, first", own_first_stab = "own times, first, stabilised",
            own_cens = "own times, cens", common_grid_first = "own times on the full grid")
rows <- lapply(versions, function(v) {
  bv <- stored$by_version[[v]]
  st <- if (!isTRUE(bv$installed) || is.null(bv$results)) rep("could not be run", length(labels)) else
    vapply(names(labels), function(nm) status(bv$results[[nm]], refs[[nm]]), "")
  c(v, st)
})
rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- c(paste0("this version (", utils::packageVersion("ipw"), ")"),
  vapply(names(labels), function(nm) {
    d <- max(abs(now[[nm]] / refs[[nm]] - 1)); if (d < 1e-8) "correct" else paste0("incorrect (", fmt(d), ")")
  }, ""))
tab <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, rows), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(tab) <- c("Version", labels)
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE)
```

The numbers in brackets are the largest relative difference between a
version's weights and the correct weights (2 means one weight is three times
too large or too small). Versions 1.0 to 1.0-11 had no `type = "cens"`.

```{r identical, include = FALSE}
ok <- vapply(versions, function(v) {
  r <- old_res(v, "own_first")
  !is.null(r) && is.na(r$error) && isTRUE(all.equal(r$weights, old_res("1.0", "own_first")$weights, tolerance = 1e-10))
}, logical(1))
```

All versions are correct for the data on the full grid (`haartdat`, and
the visit-time data after splitting onto the full grid), and all
`r sum(ok)` versions give the same weights as ipw 1.0 for the data with
individual visit times, to 1e-10: the calculation was the same from the
first release, and the rewrite in 1.3 kept it.

How far off are the older versions' weights for the data with individual
visit times? For the unstabilised weights:

```{r size}
old_w <- old_res("1.3.2", "own_first")$weights
summary(old_w / refs$own_first)
c(largest_weight_old = max(old_w), largest_weight_correct = max(refs$own_first))
```

## 7. What it does to an estimate: a simulation

```{r sim-setup, include = FALSE}
sim <- readRDS("survival-weights-time-grid-sim.rds")
sc <- sim$scenarios
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
sim_rows <- function(r, label) {
  one <- function(x, method) {
    data.frame(Visits = label, Method = method,
               `Mean estimate` = pct(mean(x)),
               Bias = paste0(formatC(100 * (mean(x) - r$truth), format = "f", digits = 1, flag = "+"), "%"),
               MCSE = pct(sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)), 2),
               `Empirical SD` = pct(sd(x)),
               check.names = FALSE)
  }
  rbind(one(r$dev$results[, "naive"], "No weights"),
        one(r$old$results[, "weighted"], "Weights from ipw 1.2.1.1"),
        one(r$dev$results[, "weighted"], paste0("Weights from this version (", r$dev$version, ")")))
}
```

This simulation has a known answer. It shows what happens to an estimate
when data with individual visit times, *not* split onto the full grid, are
used with an older version, and that the updated version handles such data
directly.

**The question.** What is the risk of death within one year *if nobody
started treatment*? In the data, patients start treatment during
follow-up, and their follow-up is stopped (censored) at that moment.
Censoring weights from `ipwtm()` (`type = "cens"`) make the patients who are
still untreated stand in for those who started, and a weighted
Kaplan-Meier estimate gives the risk.

**The data.** `r sim$n` patients per data set, followed for one year.

* Each patient has their **own visit times**. At each visit a covariate `l`
  (think of a marker of disease severity) is measured; it changes from visit
  to visit and stays fixed between visits.
* Patients with a higher `l` are **more likely to start treatment** (hazard
  ratio 2.2 per unit of `l`) and **more likely to die** (hazard ratio 2.2 per
  unit).
* So the patients who stay untreated are the healthier ones, and simply
  censoring at treatment start without weights gives a risk that is
  **too low**.
* Treatment start and death happen at exact times between visits, so the
  Cox model that `ipwtm()` fits for treatment start (`~ l`) is correct.
* The true risk without treatment is computed by simulating
  400,000 patients from the same process with treatment start switched off.

The code that makes the data and runs the analysis is in
`data-raw/make-survival-time-grid-simulation.R`. Each data set is analysed like
this:

```{r sim-analysis, eval = FALSE}
w <- ipwtm(exposure = start_trt, family = "survival", denominator = ~ l,
           id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = time, type = "cens", data = d)
fit <- survfit(Surv(tstart, time, death) ~ 1, data = d, weights = w$ipw.weights)
1 - summary(fit, times = 365)$surv        # estimated 1-year risk
```

There are `r sim$R` data sets in each of two scenarios: visits 3 to 20 days
apart, and visits 1 to 5 days apart. The same data sets are analysed with
ipw 1.2.1.1 and with this version.

```{r sim-truth, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Visits = c("3 to 20 days apart", "1 to 5 days apart"),
  `True 1-year risk without treatment` = c(pct(sc$long$truth, 2), pct(sc$short$truth, 2)),
  `Rows per data set (average)` = round(c(mean(sc$long$dev$results[, "rows"]),
                                          mean(sc$short$dev$results[, "rows"]))),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lrr")
```

```{r sim-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(rbind(sim_rows(sc$long, "3 to 20 days apart"),
                   sim_rows(sc$short, "1 to 5 days apart")), row.names = FALSE)
```

MCSE is the Monte Carlo standard error of the mean estimate: a bias smaller
than about two MCSE is within simulation noise.

**What the table shows.**

* **ipw 1.2.1.1 gives exactly the same answer as no weights.** Its weights
  hardly differ from 1: on average the largest weight in a data set is
  `r round(mean(sc$long$old$results[, "max_w"]), 2)`, against
  `r round(mean(sc$long$dev$results[, "max_w"]), 1)` with the updated version.
  With exact event times, almost every row ends at its own time, and the
  "previous time in the data" that the old code used is a moment before the
  end of the row. The hazard over that moment is almost zero, so the
  probability of staying untreated is almost 1 and the weight almost 1. The
  old weights therefore did not correct for the confounding at all.
* **The updated version removes the bias.** With visits 1 to 5 days apart its
  estimate is within simulation noise of the true risk. With visits 3 to 20
  days apart a small bias remains
  (`r formatC(100 * (mean(sc$long$dev$results[, "weighted"]) - sc$long$truth), format = "f", digits = 1, flag = "+")`
  percentage points, against
  `r formatC(100 * (mean(sc$long$old$results[, "weighted"]) - sc$long$truth), format = "f", digits = 1, flag = "+")`
  for the old version). That is not related to the time grid: `ipwtm()` gives each row the
  weight at the *end* of the row, and uses it for the whole row. Within a
  long row the weight should grow gradually, so patients who are still
  followed early in the row get a slightly too large weight. This
  approximation is the same in every version, and it shrinks as rows get
  shorter, while the old version's bias does not.

**One data set.** The cumulative risk of death in the first data set
(visits 3 to 20 days apart), without weights, with the weights of ipw
1.2.1.1 (dashed), and with the weights of this version. The dotted line is the true
risk at one year.

```{r sim-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
ex <- sim$example$data
w_new <- ipwtm(exposure = start_trt, family = "survival", denominator = ~ l, id = id,
               tstart = tstart, timevar = time, type = "cens", data = ex)$ipw.weights
curves <- list(
  "No weights" = survfit(Surv(tstart, time, death) ~ 1, data = ex),
  "ipw 1.2.1.1" = survfit(Surv(tstart, time, death) ~ 1, data = ex, weights = sim$example$old_w),
  "This version" = survfit(Surv(tstart, time, death) ~ 1, data = ex, weights = w_new))
cols <- c("grey50", "#D55E00", "#0072B2")
lty <- c(1, 2, 1)
plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, 365), ylim = c(0, max(0.45, sc$long$truth + 0.05)),
     xlab = "Days", ylab = "Cumulative risk of death", las = 1)
for (k in seq_along(curves)) {
  lines(curves[[k]]$time, 1 - curves[[k]]$surv, type = "s", col = cols[k], lty = lty[k], lwd = 2)
}
abline(h = sc$long$truth, lty = 3)
legend("topleft", c(names(curves), "True risk at one year"), col = c(cols, "black"),
       lty = c(lty, 3), lwd = c(2, 2, 2, 1), bty = "n")
```

The curve with the old weights lies on top of the unweighted curve.

```{r sim-example-weights}
summary(sim$example$old_w)   # ipw 1.2.1.1
summary(w_new)               # this version
rows_affected(ex, "id", "tstart", "time", "start_trt")
nrow(ex)
```

## 8. If you used an older version

**If your data were on the full grid, your weights are correct.** This is
the case if all follow-up was split at all times that occur in the data
(for example, all event and end times of all subjects), as in the examples
of the JSS paper and Example 2 of `?ipwtm`, or if all subjects simply have
rows at the same time points, as in `haartdat`. The last column of the table
in section 6 shows that every version gives correct weights for such data.

**To be sure**, do one of these:

1. Run `rows_affected()` (section 5) on the data you gave to `ipwtm()`. If
   it returns 0, the data were on the full grid and the weights were
   correct.
2. Rerun the analysis with the updated ipw. For data on the full grid it
   gives the same weights as the older versions; the package tests check this
   against stored results of ipw 1.2.1.1. If the weights differ, the data
   were not on the full grid, and the new weights are the correct ones.

**If your data were not on the full grid**, recompute the weights with the
updated ipw, which handles individual visit times directly. With an older
version you can get correct weights by first splitting every row at all
times that occur in the data. For example:

```{r split, eval = FALSE}
split_full_grid <- function(d) {
  grid <- sort(unique(c(d$tstart, d$time)))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(d)), function(r) {
    cuts <- grid[grid > d$tstart[r] & grid < d$time[r]]
    s <- c(d$tstart[r], cuts); e <- c(cuts, d$time[r]); k <- length(s)
    data.frame(id = d$id[r], tstart = s, time = e, x = d$x[r], l = d$l[r],
               a = c(rep(0, k - 1), d$a[r]))   # exposure on the last piece only
  }))
}
```

Covariates keep the value of the original row on every piece, and the
exposure (or censoring) event goes on the last piece only. The weight at the
end of an original row is the weight on its last piece; it equals the weight
that the updated version gives for the original row.

## 9. The code: before and after

```{r show-code, include = FALSE}
show_lines <- function(x, lines) {
  x <- gsub("\t", "  ", x)
  cat(sprintf("%4d  %s", lines, x[lines]), sep = "\n")
}
```

The code below is taken from the source packages on CRAN (stored with this
article by `data-raw/make-survival-time-grid-article-data.R`); line numbers are
those of `R/ipwtm.R` in each version. Only the denominator model is shown;
the numerator model had the same code.

### ipw 1.0 (2011)

```{r code-1.0, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
show_lines(stored$old_code[["1.0"]], 147:162)
```

Line 148 makes a list of **all distinct times in the data**
(`tempdat$timevar`, the end times of all rows of all subjects). Lines
152-153 take the increase of the cumulative baseline hazard between
neighbouring times in that list, and line 155 attaches it to each row by its
end time. Lines 158-160 use that increase as the hazard of the row. The
start time of the row (`tstart`) is not used at all.

### ipw 1.2.1.1 (the last version before the rewrite)

```{r code-1.2.1.1, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
show_lines(stored$old_code[["1.2.1.1"]], 186:202)
```

The same calculation (lines 187, 191-192, 194, 197); only the censoring
weights (`type = "cens"`, line 200) were added.

### ipw 1.3.2 (CRAN, after the rewrite)

```{r code-1.3.2, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
show_lines(stored$old_code[["1.3.2"]], 491:513)
```

The rewrite kept the calculation: `u_times` is the list of all distinct end
times (line 492), `step_haz` the increase between neighbouring times (line
501), merged onto the rows by their end time and used as the hazard of the
row (line 513).

### This version

```{r code-now, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
src <- if (file.exists("../../R/ipwtm.R")) readLines("../../R/ipwtm.R") else character()
from <- grep("Hazard over each row's own interval", src)
to <- grep("inst_haz <- ", src)
if (length(from) == 1 && length(to) == 1) show_lines(src, from:to) else
  cat("(source of this version not found)\n")
```

The cumulative baseline hazard is now evaluated at both ends of each row's
own interval, `timevar` and `tstart`, and the difference is the hazard of
the row. This is the calculation that `type = "all"` (new in this version)
already used. For data on the full grid the weights are unchanged; the
package tests check this against the stored results of ipw 1.2.1.1 for
`haartdat` and other data.

### Tests

The package tests compare the weights with a baseline hazard computed by
hand from the risk sets, as in section 4, for `type = "first"` and
`type = "cens"`, on data with individual visit times, with tied times and
with follow-up starting below 0, with the rows in random order. This is the
test (from `tests/testthat/test-audit2-ipwtm.R`; the helper functions
`r2_H0()`, `r2_surv_ref()` and `r2_irregular()` are defined at the top of
that file):

```{r test-code, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
tf <- "../../tests/testthat/test-audit2-ipwtm.R"
tsrc <- if (file.exists(tf)) readLines(tf) else character()
from <- grep("^r2_H0 <- function", tsrc)
start <- grep("survival first/cens equal an independent by-hand Efron interval hazard", tsrc)
end <- if (length(start)) start - 1 + which(tsrc[start:length(tsrc)] == "})")[1] else NA
if (length(from) == 1 && length(start) == 1 && !is.na(end)) {
  cat(tsrc[from:(from + 9)], "...", tsrc[start:end], sep = "\n")
} else cat("(test file not found)\n")
```

For data with individual visit times, the same comparison fails for every
version up to 1.3.2, as section 6 shows.
Another test checks that `type = "first"` and `type = "all"` agree when every
subject is exposed at most once (`tests/testthat/test-audit-ipwtm.R`). The
tests run on Linux, macOS and Windows with every change to the package.
